# STHINCS: Optimized SPHINCS+ for Practical Signature Capacities

> Authors: C. Kusuma
>
> License: MIT

---

# Abstract

NIST [NIST Special Publication 800-230 (Initial Public Draft)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/230/ipd) serves as a technical extension of [FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)](https://www.google.com/search?client=safari&rls=en&q=FIPS+205+(SLH-DSA)&ie=UTF-8&oe=UTF-8), introducing six additional parameter sets for security levels 1, 3, and 5. These variants optimize performance by establishing a strict limit of 2²⁴ (16.8 million) signatures per signing key, targeting use cases like software, firmware, and certificate signing. While practical for these scenarios, NIST cautions that this limit is not approved for general-purpose use and requires careful operational controls.

STHINCS is a complementary, production-oriented variant of SPHINCS+ that takes a different approach to balancing signature capacity and performance. Instead of a severe 2²⁴ limit, STHINCS adopts a 2³⁰ (≈1.07 billion) signature capacity per key pair. This provides three orders of magnitude more signatures than the NIST reduced variants while still achieving 38–58% smaller signatures than the standard 2⁶⁴ SPHINCS+ parameter sets.


## 1. Comparison with NIST Standard SPHINCS+

The table below places STHINCS directly against the NIST FIPS 205 / SPHINCS+ reference values. Key sizes are unchanged; all savings come from the reduced hypertree height (H=30 vs H=60–68).

| SHA2-128s-simple | NIST Level 1 | 32 | 64 | 7,856 | 4,864 | **−38.1%** |
| SHA2-192f-robust | NIST Level 3 | 48 | 96 | 35,664 | 15,216 | **−57.3%** |

| SHA2-256s-simple | NIST Level 5 | 64 | 128 | 29,792 | 16,384 | **−45.0%** |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SHAKE-128f-robust | NIST Level 1 | 32 | 64 | 17,088 | 7,216 | **−57.8%** |

> Signature sizes for STHINCS SHAKE variants are identical to the SHA-2 variants at the same N and f/s configuration — size depends only on the tree structure, not the hash function.

**Summary of savings:**
- Fast variants (`f`): signature size reduced by **~50–58%**
- Slow variants (`s`): signature size reduced by **~38–45%**
- Public key and secret key sizes: **no change**
- Security level (NIST Level 1 / 3 / 5): **no change**
- Security model (NA-EUF-CMA): **no change**

## 3. Background: SPHINCS+ and the `2^64` Problem

SPHINCS+ is a stateless hash-based signature scheme standardized by NIST as FIPS 205. "Stateless" means the scheme does not require tracking which leaf indices have been used — the message digest itself determines which leaf to sign with, making key management straightforward and eliminating the catastrophic failure mode of stateful schemes (XMSS, LMS) where index reuse breaks security.

The NIST standard uses a hypertree height of **H = 60 to 68**, supporting up to **2^64 signatures per key pair**:

```
2^64 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 signatures
     ≈ 584,000 years at 1,000,000 signatures/second
```

This is an astronomically conservative number. For any real-world deployment — a TLS certificate authority, a blockchain node, a firmware signing pipeline — the practical requirement is orders of magnitude smaller. The 2^64 capacity is not free: it directly inflates signature sizes, key generation time, and signing latency, since larger H means taller hypertrees and more authentication path material.


## 3.1 The Change: 2^64 → 2^30

STHINCS sets **H = 30** across all parameter sets, reducing maximum capacity to:

```
2^30 = 1,073,741,824 signatures
     ≈ 34 years at 1 signature/second
```

This single parameter change flows through the construction as follows:

| Parameter | SPHINCS+ (NIST) | STHINCS | Effect |
|-----------|-----------------|---------|--------|
| H (total tree height) | 60–68 | **30** | Halved |
| Max signatures | 2^64 | **2^30** | Reduced by 2^34 |
| Signature size | baseline | **40–50% smaller** | Fewer auth path nodes |
| Key generation | baseline | **~2× faster** | Shallower tree |
| Signing speed | baseline | **~2× faster** | Less path computation |

**Nothing else changes.** N, W, K, LogT, D, and the security proofs are all preserved. The reduction is purely in the height of the virtual hypertree.

### 3.2 What `H` Controls

The hypertree in SPHINCS+ is a virtual structure of height H, split into D layers of real XMSS trees each of height H' = H/D. Each leaf corresponds to one possible signature. The index of the leaf to use is derived deterministically from the message digest, so no state is needed.

Reducing `H` from `64` to `30` means:
- Fewer total leaves `(2^30 instead of 2^64)`
- Shorter authentication paths in each XMSS tree
- Smaller signature output
- No change to the one-wayness or collision-resistance requirements of the underlying hash function

All benchmarks measured on consistent hardware across 18 parameter set variants. SPHINXHASH is a custom hash function optimized for the SPHINCS+ construction.

Key sizes are the same across all hash function variants and f/s configurations at the same N.


## 5. Parameter Sets Reference

All parameter sets use H=30. The table below lists the internal parameters for each configuration.

| Parameter Set | N | W | H | D | H' | K | LogT | T |
|---------------|---|---|---|---|-----|---|------|---|
| {hash}-256f | 32 | 16 | 30 | 6 | 5 | 35 | 9 | 512 |
| {hash}-256s | 32 | 16 | 30 | 3 | 10 | 20 | 13 | 8192 |
| {hash}-192f | 24 | 16 | 30 | 6 | 5 | 33 | 8 | 256 |
| {hash}-192s | 24 | 16 | 30 | 3 | 10 | 18 | 12 | 4096 |
| {hash}-128f | 16 | 16 | 30 | 6 | 5 | 30 | 6 | 64 |
| {hash}-128s | 16 | 16 | 30 | 3 | 10 | 14 | 11 | 2048 |

**Parameter definitions:**

- **N** — Hash output length in bytes. Controls security level.
- **W** — Winternitz parameter. Fixed at 16 (must be a power of 2).
- **H** — Total hypertree height. Fixed at 30. Determines max signatures (2^30).
- **D** — Number of hypertree layers. 6 for fast variants, 3 for slow variants.
- **H' = H/D** — Height of each individual XMSS tree.
- **K** — Number of FORS trees in the FORS signing layer.
- **LogT** — Log₂ of leaves per FORS tree.
- **T = 2^LogT** — Number of leaves per FORS tree.


## 5.1 API Reference

### 5.2 Constructor Functions

Each parameter set is created via a dedicated constructor. All constructors accept one boolean argument: `RANDOMIZE`.

When `RANDOMIZE = true`, signing uses a fresh random value `opt` per signature (randomized hashing). When `RANDOMIZE = false`, `opt` is set to `SK.prf` (deterministic hashing). Randomized signing provides hedged security against fault attacks and side-channel leakage; deterministic signing is reproducible.

```go
// Security Level 1 (N=32, ~128-bit post-quantum)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256256fRobust(true)   // SHA256, Fast, Robust
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256256sRobust(true)   // SHA256, Slow, Robust
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256256fSimple(true)   // SHA256, Fast, Simple
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256256sSimple(true)   // SHA256, Slow, Simple

// Security Level 3 (N=24, ~192-bit post-quantum)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256192fRobust(true)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256192sRobust(true)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256192fSimple(true)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256192sSimple(true)

// Security Level 5 (N=16, ~64-bit post-quantum — legacy, not recommended for new deployments)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256128fRobust(true)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256128sRobust(true)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256128fSimple(true)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256128sSimple(true)
```

Equivalent constructors are available for `SHAKE256` and `SPHINXHASH` variants, following the same naming pattern:

```
MakeSthincsPlusSHAKE256{bits}{f|s}{Robust|Simple}
MakeSthincsPlusSPHINXHASH{bits}{f|s}{Robust|Simple}
```

### 5.3 Generic Constructor

For custom configurations:

```go
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlus(
    n,          // Hash output length (bytes): 16, 24, or 32
    w,          // Winternitz parameter (must be power of 2): 16
    h,          // Total hypertree height: 30
    d,          // Number of hypertree layers: 3 (slow) or 6 (fast)
    k,          // Number of FORS trees
    logt,       // Log2 of FORS leaves per tree
    hashFunc,   // "SHA256-robust", "SHA256-simple", "SHAKE256-robust",
                // "SHAKE256-simple", "SPHINXHASH-robust", "SPHINXHASH-simple"
    randomize,  // true = randomized signing, false = deterministic
)
```

**Validation rules enforced at construction time:**
- `H % D == 0` — tree height must divide evenly into layers
- `W` must be a power of 2
- `LogT < 62` — prevents integer overflow in `1 << LogT`
- Computed message digest length `m >= 16` bytes


## 6. Hash Function Variants

STHINCS supports three hash function families, each available in robust and simple variants.

### 6.1 SHA256

The standard SHA-256 hash function. Well-studied, hardware-accelerated on most modern CPUs. Recommended default for general-purpose deployments.

- Signing time: moderate (108–4244 ms depending on parameter set)
- Widely available in all cryptographic libraries
- NIST-approved

### 6.2 SHAKE256

SHA-3 based extendable-output function. Provides domain separation and variable-length output natively, which maps cleanly onto the tweakable hash construction used in SPHINCS+.

- Signing time: ~40% slower than SHA256 in this implementation
- Preferred when SHA-3 compatibility is required
- NIST-approved

### 6.3 SPHINXHASH

A custom hash function optimized for the SPHINCS+ internal operations. Significantly faster than SHA256 and SHAKE256 due to reduced overhead in the tweakable hash layer.

- Signing time: **5–7× faster than SHA256** across all parameter sets
- Key generation: **5–6× faster than SHA256**
- Verification: **5–6× faster than SHA256**
- Suitable where performance is critical and the custom hash is acceptable to the deployment environment

> **Warning:** SPHINXHASH is not a NIST-standardized function. Before using it in a regulated environment, confirm that custom hash constructions are permitted by your security policy.


## 7. Robust vs Simple Variants

All parameter sets come in two tweakable hash variants:

### 7.1 Robust

The hash function inputs are XORed with a bitmask before hashing:

```
H_robust(PK.seed, ADRS, M) = H(PK.seed, ADRS, M XOR bitmask(PK.seed, ADRS))
```

This provides a stronger security proof: the scheme is secure assuming only that the underlying hash function is a secure PRF (pseudorandom function). The proof holds even if the adversary can choose the bitmask inputs adaptively.

### 7.2 Simple

No bitmask is applied:

```
H_simple(PK.seed, ADRS, M) = H(PK.seed, ADRS, M)
```

Faster, but the security proof requires a slightly stronger assumption (the hash function must behave as a random oracle in addition to being a PRF). In practice, both variants are considered secure for SHA256 and SHAKE256.

**Recommendation:** Use Robust for applications where the strongest formal security guarantee is required. Use Simple where performance is the priority and the weaker security assumption is acceptable.


## 8. Fast vs Slow Variants

The fast/slow distinction controls the trade-off between signature size and signing speed.

### 8.1 Fast Variants (suffix `f`)

- **D = 6** layers, **H' = 5** (32 leaves per XMSS tree)
- More layers → more authentication paths → **larger signatures**
- Smaller trees → faster tree traversal → **faster signing**
- Suitable for applications where low latency matters more than bandwidth

### 8.2 Slow Variants (suffix `s`)

- **D = 3** layers, **H' = 10** (1024 leaves per XMSS tree)
- Fewer layers → fewer authentication paths → **smaller signatures**
- Larger trees → slower tree traversal → **slower signing**
- Suitable for applications where signature size matters (e.g., storage, on-chain data)

| Configuration | Sign Time (SHA256) | Signature Size | Best For |
|---------------|-------------------|----------------|----------|
| 256f | 298 ms | 25,056 bytes | Low-latency signing |
| 256s | 4,244 ms | 16,384 bytes | Compact storage |
| 192f | 173 ms | 15,216 bytes | Low-latency, moderate security |
| 192s | 2,568 ms | 10,032 bytes | Compact, moderate security |
| 128f | 108 ms | 7,216 bytes | Low-latency, legacy |
| 128s | 1,680 ms | 4,864 bytes | Compact, legacy |


## 9. Signature Lifetime Analysis

STHINCS limits each key pair to **2³⁰ (1,073,741,824) signatures** — approximately 1 billion signatures. The tables below show how long this capacity lasts under different signing rates and block time scenarios.

**2³⁰ Signature Lifetime by Signing Rate**

| Signing Rate | Time to Exhaust 2³⁰ Signatures |
|--------------|-------------------------------|
| 1 signature/second | **~34 years** |
| 10 signatures/second | **~3.4 years** |
| 100 signatures/second | **~124 days** |
| 1,000 signatures/second | **~12.4 days** |
| 10,000 signatures/second | **~1.24 days** |
| 100,000 signatures/second | **~3 hours** |
| 1,000,000 signatures/second | **~18 minutes** |

**2³⁰ Signature Lifetime by Block Time (Blockchain Nodes)**

| Block Time | Signatures/Year | 2³⁰ Lifetime | Suitable For |
|------------|----------------|--------------|--------------|
| 5 minutes | 105,120 | **~10,220 years** | Bitcoin-style chains |
| 1 minute | 525,600 | **~2,044 years** | Fast blockchains |
| 30 seconds | 1,051,200 | **~1,022 years** | High-throughput chains |
| 12 seconds (Ethereum) | 2,628,000 | **~408 years** | Ethereum validators |
| 5 seconds | 6,307,200 | **~170 years** | Very fast chains |
| 1 second | 31,536,000 | **~34 years** | Extreme throughput |
| 0.5 seconds | 63,072,000 | **~17 years** | Near real-time chains |


> **Hard limit:** A key pair **must not** be used beyond 2^30 signatures. Key rotation must be planned and enforced by the application layer. STHINCS itself does not enforce this limit at runtime, as it is a stateless scheme.


## 10. Choosing a Parameter Set

Use this decision tree:

1. **What NIST security level do you need?**
   - NIST Level 1 (128-bit post-quantum): choose N=32 (`256` suffix)
   - NIST Level 3 (192-bit post-quantum): choose N=24 (`192` suffix)
   - Legacy (64-bit post-quantum): choose N=16 (`128` suffix) — not recommended for new deployments

2. **Do you prioritize signature size or signing speed?**
   - Speed: choose Fast (`f`)
   - Size: choose Slow (`s`)

3. **Which hash function?**
   - Default / regulated environments: `SHA256`
   - SHA-3 ecosystem compatibility: `SHAKE256`
   - Maximum performance / internal use: `SPHINXHASH`

4. **Robust or Simple?**
   - Strongest security proof: `Robust`
   - Maximum performance, acceptable weaker assumption: `Simple`

**Recommended defaults for new deployments:**

```go
// Best balance of security, compatibility, and performance
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256256fRobust(true)  // Level 1, fast, randomized

// Smallest signatures at Level 1
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSHA256256sRobust(true)  // Level 1, slow, randomized

// Maximum performance (internal systems)
params := parameters.MakeSthincsPlusSPHINXHASH256fSimple(true)
```
